name: Elbow dislocation
populations: people with a high-energy fall or crash
summary: Usually a posterior dislocation of the ulna and radius from a fall on the outstretched hand. Simple cases stay stable after reduction and do best with early guided movement. Fracture-dislocations need surgical review.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: In a 100-patient RCT, early motion gave a larger flexion-extension arc at 6 weeks than 3 weeks of plaster (121° vs 102°), but disability scores were the same at 1 year (DASH 4.0 vs 4.2)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; often about 2–3 months after a simple dislocation and longer after fracture-dislocation (clinical convention; no validated criteria were found)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Stability through the arc of motion after reduction, with a neurovascular check; the lateral pivot-shift apprehension test is the most sensitive test for later posterolateral rotatory instability (no accuracy figures given)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs before and after reduction to confirm congruence and exclude fracture; CT is used when a fracture is suspected (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Highest incidence at 10–19 years (6.87 per 100,000 person-years in US emergency departments)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 5.21 per 100,000 person-years in US emergency departments; males and females were equally affected

overview:
An elbow dislocation is a displacement of the ulna and radius from the humerus, nearly always posteriorly or posterolaterally. In a US emergency-department database the estimated incidence was 5.21 per 100,000 person-years, highest in adolescents aged 10–19 years, with about equal rates in males and females and nearly half of the injuries in people aged 10 or older occurring in sport [r1]. The usual mechanism is a fall on the outstretched hand with an axial load and a rotational force on the elbow, and a cadaver study showed that external rotation and valgus moments combined with axial force produce posterior dislocation [r2].

A dislocation without a fracture is called simple, and one with an associated fracture is called complex. The terrible triad is a dislocation with fractures of the radial head and coronoid process [r3]. Treatment is determined by stability after reduction [r4]. In adults with simple dislocations, early mobilisation was safe and gave faster recovery than 3 weeks of plaster, although there was no benefit at 1 year [r5]. Routine ligament repair added nothing in a small randomised trial [r6].

Simple dislocation is not entirely benign: at a mean of 88 months, 56% of patients reported residual stiffness and 62% reported residual pain [r7]. The evidence base is thin: a critical appraisal found only one level I and three level II trials, there is no consensus definition of an unstable elbow, and the best rehabilitation protocols are unsettled, especially after fracture-dislocation [r8, r9].

epidemiology.text: In the US National Electronic Injury Surveillance System, 1066 elbow dislocations represented a weighted estimate of 36,751 acute dislocations, an incidence of 5.21 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI 4.74–5.68). The highest incidence (43.5% of cases) was in those aged 10–19 years (6.87 per 100,000 person-years). The incidence rate ratio of males to females was 1.02. In people aged 10 or older, 44.5% of dislocations occurred in sport: males in football, wrestling and basketball, females in gymnastics and skating [r1]. Posterolateral and posterior directions dominate: of 64 adults with MRI after a low-energy dislocation, 53% were posterolateral, 41% posterior and 6% posteromedial [r10]. This page covers adults and adolescents; paediatric supracondylar fractures and pulled elbow are separate conditions.

intrinsic: Adolescence: the highest incidence was at 10–19 years [r1]
Generalised ligamentous laxity or earlier elbow instability (clinical reasoning; not quantified in the sources reviewed)
Sex: rates were similar in males and females (rate ratio 1.02), although the sports differ [r1]
extrinsic: Sport: nearly half of dislocations in people aged 10 or older occurred in sport, mainly football, wrestling and basketball in males and gymnastics and skating in females [r1]
A fall on the outstretched hand with the body rotating on the planted arm (modifiable through falling technique; effect untested) [r2]
High-energy trauma (road crash or fall from height) is associated with complex fracture-dislocations (clinical observation)

mechanism.summary: In a typical fall on the outstretched hand the forearm is planted while the body rotates on it, so the elbow receives an axial load with external rotation (supination) and valgus moments as it flexes. In cadaver specimens this combination produced posterior dislocation in 12 of 13 elbows, with posterolateral rotation of 34–50° and valgus of 5–23° at about 80° of flexion [r2]. Soft-tissue failure progresses from the lateral side to the medial side across three stages, with dislocation as the final stage [r2]. The coronoid then passes behind the trochlea and the olecranon sits behind the humerus. Later MRI series show that the real injury pattern is more variable than this single pathway [r11, r10].
sequence: The person falls with the arm outstretched and the elbow near-straight, and the hand strikes the ground (clinical observation).
An axial force passes up the forearm while the body rotates internally on the planted arm, so the elbow experiences external rotation and valgus moments as it begins to flex [r2].

The lateral ligament complex fails first, with the lateral ulnar collateral ligament the key lateral stabiliser lost, and the ulna and radius rotate posterolaterally away from the humerus (stage 1) [r2, r4].

Soft-tissue disruption spreads through the capsule towards the medial side (stage 2) [r2]; in MRI series the lateral collateral complex and anterior capsule were torn in all 64 dislocations and the medial collateral ligament in 91% [r10].
The coronoid clears the trochlea and the ulna and radius displace posteriorly: a complete posterior or posterolateral dislocation (stage 3) [r2].

The elbow is swollen, painful and deformed, and the olecranon is prominent behind the humerus (clinical observation); ulnar and median nerves and the brachial artery can be stretched or contused (clinical reasoning).
After reduction, stability through the arc of motion decides treatment: most simple dislocations stay stable and can move early [r4, r5].

variants.name: Posterolateral rotatory dislocation (the usual pattern)
variants.description: Most dislocations are posterior or posterolateral: 53% posterolateral and 41% posterior of 64 [r10], and 12 posterolateral and 3 posterior of 16 on radiographs in another series [r11]. The 'Horii circle' is the name often given to the lateral-to-medial progression of soft-tissue failure; the original Horii description was not retrieved for this page and the sequence is taken from O'Driscoll's work [r2].

variants.name: Medially pronounced or valgus-driven injury (reversed Horii circle)
variants.description: In 11 of 64 patients (17%) the injury was more pronounced medially than laterally, which the authors took to indicate a pure valgus mechanism that spreads from medial to anterior [r10]. In 17 prospective cases no single mechanism-related pattern was seen, so the usual sequence is a teaching model rather than a rule [r11].

variants.name: Complex dislocation (with fracture)
variants.description: Associated fractures of the radial head, coronoid, olecranon or distal humerus. The terrible triad is a dislocation with radial head and coronoid fractures [r3]. The Wrightington classification groups coronoid patterns (anteromedial facet, bifacet, with radial head, and others) and links each pattern to the soft tissues likely to be injured [r12].

variants.name: Recurrent posterolateral rotatory instability
variants.description: After a dislocation, insufficiency of the lateral ulnar collateral ligament can lead to recurrent painful clicking, snapping or locking, typically in the extension part of the arc with the forearm supinated [r13, r4].

anatomy.text: The elbow is a hinge between the trochlea and the ulna (ulnohumeral joint) with the radial head articulating against the capitellum and rotating in the annular ligament. O'Driscoll's three prerequisites for stability of the ulnohumeral articulation are an intact joint surface, the anterior band of the medial collateral ligament, and the ulnar part of the lateral collateral ligament, the lateral ulnar collateral ligament [r4]. The capsule is thin in front and behind (standard anatomy). The common flexor-pronator and common extensor origins arise from the medial and lateral epicondyles. The brachialis lies in front of the joint and the brachial artery, median nerve and ulnar nerve run close to it (standard anatomy). Muscle origins were found torn from the epicondyles in about half of the surgically explored simple dislocations in one trial [r6].

structures.name: Ulnohumeral joint (trochlea, olecranon, coronoid)
structures.role: The main bony stabiliser; an intact joint surface is one of three prerequisites for stability [r4]

structures.name: Lateral ulnar collateral ligament (lateral collateral complex)
structures.role: Stabilises against posterolateral rotation; its insufficiency underlies recurrent instability [r4]

structures.name: Anterior band of the medial collateral ligament
structures.role: Resists valgus stress; one of the three stability prerequisites [r4]

structures.name: Anterior capsule and brachialis
structures.role: Torn in all 64 dislocations in an MRI series (anterior capsule) and often with the medial and lateral origins [r10]

structures.name: Radial head and annular ligament
structures.role: Secondary stabiliser; a radial head fracture removes the lateral column and makes the injury complex [r3]

structures.name: Common flexor and extensor origins
structures.role: Dynamic stabilisers; involved in 31% and 39% of dislocations on MRI, and in all those with joint incongruity [r10]

structures.name: Ulnar and median nerves and brachial artery
structures.role: Run close to the joint and can be stretched or contused by the dislocation; ulnar neuropathy is among the complications after complex injury [r3]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
In simple dislocation the capsule and collateral ligaments fail without a fracture. In an MRI series of 64 patients, the lateral collateral ligament complex and anterior capsule were affected in all, the medial collateral ligament in 91%, the common extensor origin in 39% and the common flexor origin in 31%; all cases with joint incongruity (19%) had flexor or extensor origin involvement [r10]. A second series of 17 found complete anterior capsule tears in 12, medial collateral tears in 10 and lateral collateral tears in 9, with no single mechanism-related pattern [r11]. When 30 adults were examined under anaesthesia an average of four days after dislocation, all had medial instability and 16 had both medial and lateral instability; surgery found complete rupture or avulsion of both collateral ligaments, with muscle origins torn in about half [r6]. Despite this, non-operative treatment gave results no worse than repair [r6].

In the cadaver model, elbows dislocated with the anterior medial collateral ligament intact, and valgus laxity after reduction was no higher than in the intact specimen [r2]. Capsular scarring, haemarthrosis and prolonged immobilisation plausibly contribute to stiffness (clinical reasoning); stiffness and pain are the commonest long-term complaints, reported by 56% and 62% at a mean of 88 months [r7]. In fracture-dislocations, the fracture adds loss of bony stability and complications such as hardware problems, stiffness, instability and ulnar neuropathy; the overall reoperation rate after surgery for terrible triad injuries was 22.4% in one review [r3].

structures.name: Lateral collateral ligament complex
structures.effect: Affected in 64 of 64 simple dislocations on MRI [r10]; the lateral ulnar collateral ligament is the key stabiliser lost [r4]

structures.name: Anterior capsule
structures.effect: Torn in all 64 dislocations in one series and completely in 12 of 17 in another [r10, r11]

structures.name: Medial collateral ligament complex
structures.effect: Affected in 91% of 64 patients, and ruptured or avulsed in all surgically explored elbows in a small trial [r10, r6]

structures.name: Common extensor and flexor origins
structures.effect: Involved in 39% and 31% of dislocations and torn from the epicondyles in about half of explored elbows [r10, r6]

structures.name: Joint surface (radial head, coronoid, capitellum)
structures.effect: A fracture makes the dislocation complex; the terrible triad combines radial head and coronoid fractures with dislocation [r3]

muscles.name: Brachialis and elbow flexors
muscles.effect: Injured with the anterior capsule; they are a common source of swelling and pain, and calcification within the muscle is a recognised cause of lost motion (clinical observation)

muscles.name: Common flexor-pronator and extensor origins
muscles.effect: Partial avulsion in 31% and 39% on MRI [r10]; weakness in grip and forearm rotation follows (clinical observation)

muscles.name: Triceps and biceps
muscles.effect: Reflex guarding and arthrogenic muscle inhibition limit active movement early on (clinical reasoning)

muscles.name: Forearm and shoulder girdle muscles
muscles.effect: Disuse weakness during immobilisation and guarding; address in rehabilitation (clinical reasoning)

cellular.description: Bleeding into the joint and soft tissues, with neutrophils and macrophages clearing debris (typical ligament and capsule biology).
Fibroblasts lay down disorganised collagen in the torn ligaments and capsule; excessive or prolonged immobilisation promotes capsular fibrosis (typical biology).
Collagen aligns along the lines of load; controlled motion supports organised repair (typical biology).

Bone can form in injured soft tissue; the overall incidence after surgical repair of elbow fractures was 28.7%, and higher after terrible triad and elbow fracture-dislocation than after distal humerus fractures [r14].

systems.effect: Ulnar neuropathy is one of the complications after fracture-dislocation surgery [r3]; the ulnar and median nerves can also be contused by the dislocation (clinical reasoning).
Brachial artery injury is rare but limb-threatening; examine pulses and capillary return before and after reduction (clinical convention).
Haemarthrosis and soft-tissue swelling cause pain and block movement; they usually resolve within weeks (clinical observation).
The shoulder and wrist stiffen or weaken during immobilisation and guarding; keep them moving (clinical observation).
Fear of re-dislocation and apprehension can limit movement; female sex and flexion loss predicted worse patient-reported outcomes [r7].

grading.system: Simple versus complex dislocation, with the soft-tissue stages of posterolateral rotatory instability

grades.description: Ligament and capsular injury without an associated fracture on radiographs. Simple dislocation is the group included in the main randomised trials of early motion and of surgical repair [r5, r6].
grades.prognosis: Generally favourable: mean DASH 6.7 and Oxford Elbow Score 90.3 at 88 months, but 56% reported stiffness and 8% subjective instability [r7].

grades.description: Dislocation with a fracture of the radial head, coronoid, olecranon or distal humerus. The terrible triad is a dislocation with radial head and coronoid fractures [r3]; the Wrightington classification groups coronoid patterns [r12].
grades.prognosis: Functional scores are usually satisfactory but complications are common: mean Mayo Elbow Performance Scores 78–95 and a reoperation rate of 22.4% across 16 studies [r3].

grades.grade: Stages of posterolateral rotatory instability (soft-tissue spectrum)
grades.description: Posterolateral rotatory instability is a spectrum of three stages according to the degree of soft-tissue disruption, progressing from lateral to medial; dislocation is the final stage [r2, r13]. MRI series show that individual injury patterns vary [r11, r10].
grades.prognosis: Recurrent instability, when it develops, is usually due to insufficiency of the lateral ulnar collateral ligament [r4].

timeframes.summary: A stable simple dislocation heals through the standard ligament and capsule cascade, but recovery of movement is the limiting factor: with early mobilisation the flexion-extension arc was 121° at 6 weeks versus 102° after 3 weeks of plaster, and by 1 year DASH scores did not differ [r5]. Patients returned to work after about 10 days with early mobilisation versus 18 days with plaster [r5]. Fracture-dislocations follow the surgeon's protocol and recover more slowly.

healing.description: Swelling, bruising and pain; reduction, stability check and the start of gentle movement as comfort allows (typical biology; early motion protocol [r5])
Collagen repair in the ligaments and capsule; the early-mobilisation group reached an arc of 121° by 6 weeks [r5]
Collagen aligns with load; strength, endurance and function return progressively (typical biology)
Three weeks of plaster gave inferior early motion and slower return to work than immediate motion in an RCT [r5]

milestones.label: Reduction, stability check and neurovascular exam
milestones.note: Radiographs before and after; stability through the arc of motion decides treatment [r4]

milestones.label: Return to work in the early-motion group (mean)
milestones.note: 10 days versus 18 days after plaster in the FuncSiE trial [r5]

milestones.label: 6-week review: arc of motion
milestones.note: Mean arc 121° with early motion versus 102° with 3 weeks of plaster [r5]

milestones.label: Return to contact or overhead sport (typical)
milestones.note: Criteria-based, roughly 2–3 months after a simple dislocation (clinical convention)

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based, not date-based. After a simple dislocation, return to contact sport is often around 2–3 months once motion, strength and stability are near normal (clinical convention; no validated criteria were identified). After surgery for a fracture-dislocation, return follows the surgeon's protocol and may take 4–6 months or longer (clinical convention). Return to work was about 10 days with early mobilisation versus 18 days after plaster in one RCT, which reflects desk and light duties [r5].

symptoms: Sudden severe elbow pain after a fall on the outstretched hand, often with a feeling of the elbow giving way (clinical observation)
Inability to bend or straighten the elbow and an obvious deformity
Swelling and later bruising around the elbow and forearm
Numbness, tingling or weakness in the hand if a nerve is stretched or contused (clinical reasoning)
After reduction: stiffness and pain in the following weeks, with residual stiffness in 56% and residual pain in 62% at a mean of 88 months [r7]
signs: Deformity with a prominent olecranon behind the humerus and the forearm held semi-flexed (posterior dislocation; clinical observation)
Gross swelling and loss of the normal triangular relationship of the epicondyles and olecranon (clinical observation)
Loss of active and passive range of motion
Altered pulses, capillary return or sensation if neurovascular structures are involved (clinical reasoning)
After reduction, instability through the arc of motion, which determines treatment [r4]

subjective: Mechanism: fall on the outstretched hand, sport or high-energy trauma; the direction of force and any rotation [r2]
Earlier dislocation, clicking, snapping or locking, which suggests chronic posterolateral rotatory instability [r13]
Hand dominance, occupation, sport and goals; age and activity level
Symptoms since reduction: stiffness, pain, catching, giving way, numbness or tingling
Time since injury and the treatment so far (immobilisation, sling, surgery)
Associated injuries: wrist, distal radius, shoulder, head and neck (clinical convention)
observation: Carrying angle, swelling, bruising and elbow posture compared with the other side (clinical convention)
Skin integrity and any wound (open dislocation or fracture)
Willingness to move the arm; muscle guarding and protective patterns
Wrist and hand posture and colour
palpation: Medial and lateral epicondyles and olecranon: normal triangle relationship once reduced (clinical convention)
Radial head and coronoid region for tenderness suggesting a fracture
Lateral collateral and medial collateral ligament origins and common flexor and extensor origins [r10]
Distal radius, scaphoid, forearm and clavicle for associated injuries (clinical convention)
rangeOfMotion: Active flexion and extension, comparing with the other side; flexion loss predicted a poorer DASH score at long-term review [r7]
Pronation and supination at 90° of flexion, including whether motion is smooth or blocked
Look for a mechanical block, a clunk or catching, which suggests loose bone or a joint that is not congruent (clinical convention)
strength: Resisted elbow flexion and extension, forearm pronation and supination (later stages)
Grip dynamometry and wrist flexion and extension strength
Shoulder and scapular strength, which often weakens in guarding (clinical convention)
neuro: Radial pulse and capillary return before and after any reduction (clinical convention)
Median (including anterior interosseous), ulnar and radial (including posterior interosseous) nerve function and sensation; ulnar neuropathy is a recognised complication [r3]
functional: Daily tasks: dressing, carrying, pushing up from a chair (a stand-up test with the hand beside the body reproduces symptoms of posterolateral rotatory instability [r13])
Sport- or work-specific tasks, weight-bearing through the hand and catching
Patient-reported outcomes: DASH, Oxford Elbow Score, Mayo Elbow Performance Index [r5, r7]

specialTests.name: Post-reduction stability through the arc of motion
specialTests.purpose: Decide whether early guided movement is safe
specialTests.procedure: After reduction, the treating clinician moves the elbow through flexion and extension and notes whether, and at what position, it subluxates, with attention to valgus stability. O'Driscoll's cadaver study suggested reduction in supination and valgus testing in pronation, with the anterior band of the medial collateral ligament presumed intact if the elbow is stable [r2].
specialTests.positive: Re-subluxation or an unstable arc: treatment is determined by stability after reduction [r4]. A consensus definition of an unstable simple dislocation is still lacking [r8]. No accuracy figures were identified.

specialTests.name: Lateral pivot-shift apprehension test
specialTests.purpose: Detect chronic posterolateral rotatory instability after a dislocation
specialTests.procedure: With the patient supine, the examiner guides the supinated forearm into valgus and axial compression while flexing the elbow from extension, watching for apprehension or subluxation.
specialTests.positive: Apprehension (the most sensitive of the tests) or a clunk as the radial head reduces; reproducing actual subluxation usually needs general anaesthesia or an intra-articular local anaesthetic [r13]. No accuracy figures were identified in the abstract reviewed.

specialTests.name: Posterolateral rotatory drawer test and stand-up (Regan) test
specialTests.procedure: Drawer test: a rotatory version of the knee drawer test. Stand-up test: the patient pushes up from a chair with the arms at the side and the forearms supinated.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of the patient's symptoms (the stand-up test) or subluxation (the drawer test) [r13]. A lateral stress radiograph can show the rotatory subluxation [r13]. No accuracy figures were identified.

specialTests.name: Neurovascular examination
specialTests.purpose: Detect nerve or arterial injury before and after reduction
specialTests.procedure: Palpate the radial pulse, check capillary return and test median, ulnar and radial nerve sensation and motor function, including the finger flexors and extensors.
specialTests.positive: Absent pulse, a cool pale hand, or new sensory or motor loss. This is standard practice (clinical convention); no accuracy figures apply.

clinicalRules.name: Stability-based treatment principle
clinicalRules.description: Treatment is determined by the stability of the elbow after reduction; with a fracture, the principle is to fix the bones so that only the ligaments limit stability and then repair the ligaments if the elbow is still too unstable for early motion [r4]. No validated decision rule defines an unstable simple dislocation [r8].

outcomeMeasures.name: DASH or QuickDASH
outcomeMeasures.use: Primary outcome in the FuncSiE trial; 4.0 vs 4.2 at 1 year [r5]; mean 6.7 at 88 months [r7]

outcomeMeasures.name: Oxford Elbow Score
outcomeMeasures.use: Patient-rated elbow function, pain and psychosocial score; mean 90.3 at 88 months [r7]

outcomeMeasures.name: Mayo Elbow Performance Index or Score
outcomeMeasures.use: Used in the trial and in terrible triad reviews: mean MEPS 78–95 across 16 studies [r5, r3]

outcomeMeasures.name: Elbow flexion-extension arc (goniometer)
outcomeMeasures.use: Range of motion recovers more quickly with early motion (121° vs 102° at 6 weeks) and predicts later disability [r5, r7]

outcomeMeasures.name: Return-to-work and activity resumption
outcomeMeasures.use: Time to work (10 vs 18 days in FuncSiE) and sports return [r5]

imaging.indication: Before reduction to confirm the dislocation and exclude fracture, and after reduction to confirm congruence (clinical convention)
imaging.findings: Show the direction of dislocation and associated fractures (radial head, coronoid, olecranon, distal humerus); joint widening or a fleck of bone suggests an incongruent or complex injury (clinical convention). Direction in two series: mostly posterolateral or posterior [r10, r11]. A lateral stress radiograph can demonstrate rotatory subluxation in chronic instability [r13].

imaging.indication: Suspected coronoid, radial head or other fracture; surgical planning for fracture-dislocation (clinical convention)
imaging.findings: Shows the fracture pattern, for example the coronoid facet pattern that underpins the Wrightington classification [r12].

imaging.indication: Persistent instability, an incongruent joint after reduction or surgical planning; not routine for a stable simple dislocation (clinical convention)
imaging.findings: In 64 patients the lateral collateral complex and anterior capsule were torn in all, the medial collateral ligament in 91%, and the flexor and extensor origins in 31% and 39% [r10]. Whether MRI findings should change management is not established in the sources reviewed.

differentials.name: Radial head fracture (isolated)
differentials.distinguishing: Lateral elbow pain after a fall with a block to rotation but a located joint on radiographs; the fat pad sign is present.

differentials.name: Supracondylar humerus fracture (children)
differentials.distinguishing: A child with swelling and deformity above the elbow after a fall; radiographs show the fracture. The paediatric pattern differs from adult dislocation.

differentials.name: Elbow ulnar collateral ligament injury
differentials.distinguishing: Medial elbow pain in a thrower, with valgus laxity and no dislocation.

differentials.name: Triceps tendon rupture or olecranon fracture
differentials.distinguishing: A palpable defect or fleck sign at the olecranon after a fall, with weak extension and a located joint.

differentials.name: Monteggia or other forearm fracture-dislocation
differentials.distinguishing: A fracture of the proximal ulna with radial head dislocation; radiographs show an ulnar fracture and the radiocapitellar line does not pass through the capitellum.

differentials.name: Distal humerus fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Pain and swelling over the distal humerus after a fall or direct blow, with crepitus and an incongruent joint on radiographs.

differentials.name: Pulled elbow (very young children)
differentials.distinguishing: A child aged about 1–4 years refusing to use the arm after a pull, with no swelling or deformity.

redFlags: Absent or weak radial pulse, a cool, pale or mottled hand, or severe forearm pain and tense swelling after dislocation or reduction: suspect brachial artery injury or compartment syndrome and send to emergency the same day (clinical convention).

New numbness or weakness in the hand, or loss of finger and thumb movement, before or after reduction: suspect median, ulnar or radial nerve injury and refer urgently; ulnar neuropathy is a known complication [r3].
Open wound over the elbow, or a fracture seen on radiographs (radial head, coronoid, olecranon or distal humerus): complex injury, so refer to orthopaedics the same day [r3].
A suspected dislocation that has not been reduced: this is an emergency requiring prompt reduction under analgesia or sedation and neurovascular review (clinical convention).
Redislocation, a block to movement or recurrent clunking after reduction: suspect instability, an incongruent joint or a loose fragment, and refer back to the treating surgeon [r4, r13].
Progressive loss of motion over weeks, with a firm end-feel or a lump: suspect heterotopic ossification or capsular contracture and refer for radiographs and surgical review [r14].

management.principles: Treat the injury as a stability problem. After urgent reduction, the choice between early motion and surgery depends on stability through the arc of motion [r4]. For simple dislocations, an RCT of 100 adults found early mobilisation was safe (no recurrent dislocation), gave better function at 6 weeks and faster return to work, and was no worse at 1 year than 3 weeks of plaster [r5]; a critical appraisal agrees that conservative care is the standard for stable elbows and that shorter immobilisation is favoured [r8]. Routine ligament repair did not help in a randomised trial or in a retrospective comparison [r6, r15]. Complex injuries need surgical review: terrible triad surgery usually gives satisfactory scores but with complications and reoperation in about one in five [r3]. Rehabilitation protocols after fracture-dislocation are not agreed and no protocol has been shown to be best [r9]. The physiotherapist's roles are to confirm safe medical review, start early guided movement when permitted, restore function and detect warning signs.

medical.name: Urgent closed reduction with neurovascular check and radiographs
medical.description: Reduce under analgesia or sedation and check the pulse and nerves before and after. In O'Driscoll's cadaver study, posterior dislocations were proposed to be reduced in supination, and valgus stability tested in pronation [r2]. Confirm congruent reduction and look for fractures on radiographs.

medical.name: Short sling or brief immobilisation with early active motion for stable simple dislocations
medical.description: In a 100-patient RCT (48 early motion, 52 plaster for 3 weeks), early mobilisation gave a larger arc at 6 weeks (121° vs 102°), less disability (DASH 12 vs 19), earlier return to work (10 vs 18 days) and no recurrent dislocations; 1-year DASH was 4.0 vs 4.2 [r5]. The cost analysis found 10 vs 18 days of absence and total costs of €3624 vs €7072 (p = 0.094) [r16]. A retrospective comparison of 42 patients also favoured a sling and early motion (return to work 3.2 vs 6.6 weeks; no redislocation) [r17].

medical.name: Routine surgical ligament repair for simple dislocation
medical.description: In a prospective randomised study of 30 adults, repair of the ruptured collateral ligaments gave results that were not better than non-surgical treatment [r6]. A retrospective follow-up of 62 patients (28 repaired, 34 treated non-surgically) likewise found no respect in which surgery was better and no evidence to recommend primary surgical treatment of the ligament injuries [r15]. A critical appraisal notes that an unstable simple dislocation may benefit from surgery and different techniques show similar outcomes, but the definition of 'unstable' is not agreed [r8].

medical.name: Surgery for complex dislocation (fracture-dislocation, terrible triad)
medical.description: The principle is to fix the bones so that only ligaments limit stability, then repair them if the elbow remains too unstable for early motion [r4]. A review of 16 studies (312 patients) found satisfactory scores (mean MEPS 78–95) but a reoperation rate of 22.4%, mainly hardware problems, stiffness, instability and ulnar neuropathy, with heterotopic ossification in 12.5% as a complication that did not need reoperation [r3]. For the radial head, replacement and reconstruction gave similar scores (MEPS 88.6 vs 88.5) and similar reoperation (18.4% vs 17.9%) in a meta-analysis of 9 studies, with high overall complications (65%) [r18]. The evidence is observational.

medical.name: Reconstruction or repair of the lateral ulnar collateral ligament for recurrent instability
medical.description: Recurrent instability is usually due to lateral ulnar collateral ligament insufficiency, and reconstruction typically corrects it [r4]; the choice follows persistent instability rather than the first dislocation [r13].

physio.name: Early active, guided elbow movement within a stable range
physio.description: Start active flexion, extension and forearm rotation soon after reduction as pain and stability allow, with a sling for comfort. In the FuncSiE trial 'immediate motion exercises' gave a larger arc at 6 weeks and earlier work return with no recurrent dislocations and no evidence of benefit at 1 year [r5]. The exact exercise dose was not compared in the trial, so the programme is clinician-set (clinical reasoning).

physio.name: Prolonged plaster or rigid immobilisation
physio.description: Three weeks of plaster gave worse motion and slower recovery at 6 weeks than immediate motion [r5]; shorter immobilisation is favoured [r8]. Immobilisation also raises the stiffness risk, which was the commonest long-term complaint [r7].

physio.name: Forearm positioning and a hinged brace for lateral or medial instability
physio.description: O'Driscoll's cadaver study proposed testing valgus stability in pronation and, if stable, starting rehabilitation in a hinged cast-brace in full pronation [r2]. This was not tested in a trial.

physio.name: Rehabilitation after surgery for fracture-dislocation (follow the surgeon)
physio.description: Protocols vary: in 36 articles (1123 elbows) physical therapy most often began at 7 days, passive motion at 7 days and active motion at 21 days; early passive motion (within 7 days) was not associated with better range of motion or MEPS [r9]. No protocol has proved superior, so follow the surgeon's limits.

physio.name: Education, swelling control and neighbouring-joint movement
physio.description: Explain the injury and the expected stiffness, use elevation and ice, keep the shoulder, wrist and hand moving and teach warning signs (clinical convention). Stiffness and pain are common long term, so set realistic expectations [r7].

physio.name: Forceful passive stretching or manipulation
physio.description: Aggressive passive stretching of a painful, swollen elbow risks more bleeding, pain and loss of movement (clinical reasoning). No trial has tested it for dislocation, and heterotopic ossification is a known complication of elbow fractures and fracture-dislocation [r14]. Use active, graded movement instead.

physio.name: Progressive strengthening, proprioceptive and sport-specific retraining
physio.description: Restore strength and control through graded loading after motion returns (clinical convention). No trial of strengthening after elbow dislocation was identified in the sources reviewed.

education: A dislocated elbow has been put back, but the ligaments and capsule were torn. They usually heal well without surgery in simple cases.
Moving the elbow early, within comfort and as directed, usually gives faster recovery than keeping it in a cast.
Stiffness and some discomfort are common for months; in one long-term study 56% still noticed stiffness, so keep doing your exercises [r7].
Do not push or stretch the elbow forcefully. Gentle, active movement is better.
Tell us straight away about numbness, a cold or pale hand, a new deformity or the elbow slipping again.
A broken bone with the dislocation (such as a terrible triad) usually needs an operation and a slower, surgeon-led recovery [r3].

rehab.overview: Rehabilitation here is stability- and criteria-based. For stable simple dislocations, start early active movement and progress as the arc of motion, pain and strength allow. After surgery for fracture-dislocation or after an unstable dislocation, follow the surgeon's protocol, because no protocol has proved best [r9]. Early motion improved the arc at 6 weeks but not 1-year disability, so function, not speed, is the goal [r5]. Dosages are typical clinical ranges, not trial prescriptions. As a working rule (clinical convention), pain during movement should stay at or below about 3/10 and settle within hours, and swelling should not rise the next day.

stages.name: Protect & start moving
stages.timeframe: Days 0–14 (or as set by the surgeon)
goals: Begin active elbow movement within the stable arc
Keep the shoulder, wrist and hand moving
precautions: No forced passive stretching or manipulation
Avoid heavy lifting and weight-bearing through the hand
Avoid positions that reproduce a sense of the elbow slipping (clinical convention)
Refer back urgently for neurovascular change, redislocation or a block to motion [r4]

exercises.name: Gravity-assisted elbow extension and active flexion (arm hanging)
exercises.dosage: 10 repetitions every waking hour in comfortable range (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Smooth and pain-limited; do not force the last degrees

exercises.name: Active forearm pronation and supination with the elbow at 90°
exercises.cues: Elbow tucked into the side; no resistance

exercises.name: Hand and finger movement with gentle grip squeeze
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10 holds of 5 s, hourly while awake
exercises.cues: Pump the hand to reduce swelling

exercises.name: Shoulder and scapular movement (wall slide)
exercises.cues: Keep the elbow relaxed and supported

exercises.name: Elevation and swelling management
exercises.dosage: Between exercise sessions through the day
exercises.cues: Raise the hand above the elbow and elbow above the heart

progressionCriteria: Pain at or below about 3/10 at rest and on movement
Safe, stable active arc with no clunking or giving way

stages.name: Restore range
goals: Normalise daily use of the arm
precautions: Progress movement by active-assisted work, not forced stretching
Avoid heavy resistance and end-range stretching into pain
Stop if swelling or pain rises the next day or if a mechanical block appears

exercises.name: Active-assisted elbow flexion and extension (table slide with a towel)
exercises.cues: Use the other hand to help; stop at gentle tension

exercises.name: Active pronation and supination at 90° with a light bar
exercises.cues: Elbow supported and tucked in

exercises.name: Isometric elbow flexion and extension at mid-range
exercises.dosage: 5 × 10 s at about 30–50% effort, 1–2 times a day (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Steady push; no pain

exercises.name: Scapular retraction with a light band (elbow at the side)
exercises.cues: Keep the elbow close to the body

exercises.name: Wrist flexion and extension with a light dumbbell (forearm supported)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 12, 3 s up and down, 3 times a week
exercises.cues: Elbow supported on a table

progressionCriteria: Active flexion-extension arc at least about 100–110° and improving (clinical convention; early-motion mean 121° at 6 weeks [r5])
No new instability, clunking or block
Pain at or below 2/10 at rest

stages.name: Build strength & control
goals: Restore elbow, forearm and shoulder strength
Re-establish load tolerance for weight-bearing through the hand
precautions: Increase load only when the previous session settles within 24 hours
Avoid sudden valgus or hyperextension loads
After surgery for fracture-dislocation, confirm union and clearance with the surgeon before loading

exercises.name: Biceps curl and triceps extension with progressive load
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10–12, 3 s lowering, 3 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Full range, slow control; stop short of end-range pain

exercises.name: Band row and scapular strengthening
exercises.cues: Control the lowering and keep the elbow at the side

exercises.name: Wall or incline push-up
exercises.cues: Keep the elbows in line and avoid hyperextension at the top

exercises.name: Forearm pronation and supination with a weighted hammer
exercises.cues: Short lever first, then lengthen

exercises.name: Shoulder flexion raise
exercises.cues: Neutral spine and relaxed neck

progressionCriteria: Full or near-full active range compared with the other side
Elbow strength about 80% or more of the other side (clinical convention)
No pain above 2/10 and no next-day flare after loading
Stable elbow with no apprehension on loaded movements

stages.name: Return to sport and work
goals: Return to contact, catching and weight-bearing in graded steps
Restore full work and sport demands
precautions: Progress in small steps, with a next-day symptom check
Delay contact and collision sports until criteria are met
After fracture-dislocation follow the surgeon's timing and criteria

exercises.name: Weight-bearing progression (plank on the hands, quadruped, bird-dog)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 20–30 s, building to 60 s, 3 times a week
exercises.cues: Keep the elbows soft and the shoulders stable

exercises.name: Catch-and-release and ball-reaction drills
exercises.cues: Soft hands; stop if the elbow feels unstable

exercises.name: Push-up and pressing progression
exercises.cues: Full control through the full range

exercises.name: Controlled falling and landing drills (mat) for contact and gymnastics sports
exercises.dosage: 2–3 sets of 5, building height and speed, 2 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Absorb with flexed arms and roll; avoid locked elbows

exercises.name: Heavy strength maintenance (curl, row, press)
exercises.cues: Slow tempo, full range

progressionCriteria: Full pain-free range and strength about 90% or more of the other side (clinical convention)
Completes full training or work for at least 2 weeks without a flare
No apprehension, giving way or clunk on loaded or catching drills
Surgeon or physician clearance for contact

criteria: No validated return-to-sport criteria for elbow dislocation were identified in the sources reviewed; the criteria below reflect clinical convention
Full or near-full, pain-free range of motion compared with the other side, because flexion loss predicts poorer long-term function [r7]
Strength about 90% or more of the other arm (clinical convention) and no apprehension on loaded or catching tasks
A stable elbow on clinical testing, with no clunking or giving way
Tolerates graded sport-specific loading, including weight-bearing and catching, for at least 2 weeks with no flare
After fracture-dislocation, radiographic union and surgeon clearance
tests: Elbow flexion-extension and forearm rotation range compared with the other side [r7]
Grip and elbow strength dynamometry or hand-held dynamometry
Valgus and posterolateral rotatory apprehension testing by the treating clinician [r13]
DASH, Oxford Elbow Score and Mayo Elbow Performance Index [r5]
Sport-specific weight-bearing, catching and landing drills with a next-day symptom log

prognosis: For simple dislocations, outcomes are generally favourable but not benign. In 110 adults reviewed at a mean of 88 months, mean DASH was 6.7 and Oxford Elbow Score 90.3, but 56% reported residual stiffness, 62% residual pain and 8% subjective instability; loss of flexion and female sex independently predicted a worse DASH [r7]. In the FuncSiE trial, disability was the same at 1 year with early motion or plaster (DASH 4.0 vs 4.2) and no recurrent dislocations occurred in either group [r5]. After fracture-dislocation, scores are usually satisfactory (mean MEPS 78–95) but complications are common, reoperation is about 22.4% and heterotopic ossification occurred in 12.5% [r3]. The overall incidence of heterotopic ossification after surgical repair of elbow fractures is about 28.7%, higher after terrible triad injuries than after distal humerus fractures [r14]. Recurrent instability, when it occurs, is usually due to lateral ulnar collateral ligament insufficiency [r4].
prevention: No trial-proven prevention programme for elbow dislocation was identified in the sources reviewed.

Falling technique training for contact, gymnastics and skating athletes may reduce the chance of landing on a locked, outstretched arm (expert opinion; not tested in the sources reviewed). Nearly half of dislocations in people aged 10 or older occurred in sport [r1].

After a first dislocation, complete rehabilitation and restore full motion and strength before return to sport, because recurrent instability is usually due to lateral ulnar collateral ligament insufficiency [r4].
Protective padding and bracing in high-risk sports are used in practice, but their effect on elbow dislocation was not tested in the sources reviewed (clinical observation).
clinicalPearls: Stability decides treatment. Treat after reduction according to stability through the arc of motion; most simple dislocations are stable and do better with early motion than with 3 weeks of plaster [r4, r5].
An elbow dislocation is not benign. At a mean of 88 months 56% still reported stiffness and 62% pain, and loss of flexion predicted worse function, so protect range from the first week [r7].
The Horii circle is a teaching model, not a rule. In 17 prospective MRIs there was no single mechanism-related pattern, and 17% of 64 patients had medially pronounced injury [r11, r10].

An incongruent joint after reduction suggests extensive soft-tissue injury or a fracture: all 12 incongruent cases in one MRI series had flexor or extensor origin involvement, so get the surgeon to review them [r10].
Be honest about the evidence. After terrible triad surgery, early passive motion within 7 days was not associated with better motion or MEPS, and no protocol has been proved superior [r9].
Check the nerves and pulse. Ulnar neuropathy is a recognised complication, so document nerve and vascular status at every early visit [r3].

forces.label: Axial load with rotation and valgus

captions.text: A young athlete is running when a trip sends them forward.
The arm shoots out to break the fall and the elbow is near-straight.
The hand lands; force passes up the forearm into the elbow.
As the body rotates over the planted arm, the elbow takes rotation and valgus on top of the axial load.
The joint is forced past its limits and the forearm bones are driven backwards.
The elbow is painful, swollen and deformed, and the arm cannot be moved.
Zooming into the right elbow from the outer side.
On the outer side, the lateral ulnar collateral ligament holds the forearm bones against the humerus.
Axial load with supination and valgus tries to rotate the forearm bones away from the humerus.
The lateral ligament complex fails first.
The ulna and radius begin to rotate and slide backwards off the humerus.
Bleeding fills the joint as the capsule and ligaments tear.

actions.text: Forearm bones displaced behind the humerus

captions.text: On the inner side, the anterior band of the medial collateral ligament resists valgus.
As the force continues, the soft-tissue injury spreads from lateral towards medial.
The medial ligament is torn in most dislocations, partly or completely.
The coronoid clears the trochlea and the ulna and radius displace behind the humerus.
The ulnar and median nerves and the brachial artery run close and can be stretched or bruised.
Reduction puts the bones back, but the ligaments and capsule are still torn.
Most simple dislocations are then stable enough for early, guided movement.
Healthy collateral ligament: aligned type I collagen.
Under the force of the fall the fibres straighten.
The load exceeds what the collagen can bear.
The fibres fail and the ligament tears.
Bleeding fills the gap.
Inflammatory cells clear debris and signal for repair.
Fibroblasts lay down new, disorganised collagen across the tear.
Collagen remodels along the lines of load; guided early movement supports organised repair and limits stiffness.
